young.html: Albert Einstein was a scientist who asked questions a child might ask, and then kept asking. One was: what would I see if I could ride along with a beam of light? His answers changed how we think about space and time.

He wrote a short book to explain his ideas to ordinary readers, using trains, lightning and clocks. Here is the surprising part. Light always travels at the same speed, about 300,000 kilometers every second, for everyone, however fast they are moving. To make that work, time itself must run differently for people moving past each other.

Picture a clock made of light: a flash bounces up and down between two mirrors, and each bounce is one tick. Now put the clock on a speeding train. To you, standing beside the track, the flash has to travel on a slanted zigzag, a longer path. Light can’t go faster, so each tick takes longer. The moving clock runs slow!

young.name: gb-light-clock
young.cap: Press Play. The moving clock’s flash runs a longer, slanted path, so it ticks fewer times. Slide the speed up close to the speed of light.

young.html: Walking on a moving walkway. If you walk at 1 meter per second on an airport walkway that moves at 1 meter per second, a person standing still sees you going 2 meters per second. That is how speeds add for slow things. Einstein found that the rule breaks down near the speed of light: nothing, not even a beam of light from a moving train, goes faster than light. With a grown-up, look up how long light takes to reach us from the Sun (about 8 minutes).

These effects are far too small to notice at the speed of a car or a plane. But they are real. The satellites of the GPS system have to correct their clocks for them, or your map would drift by kilometers a day.

full.html: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) published his special theory of relativity in 1905, while working as a patent examiner in Bern, Switzerland. Ten years later, in November 1915, he completed the general theory, a new account of gravity. In 1916 he wrote a short popular book, Relativity: The Special and the General Theory, for readers interested in the ideas but not trained in the mathematics, as his preface explains. Robert W. Lawson’s English translation appeared in 1920, just after a British eclipse expedition, led by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson, had confirmed one of the theory’s predictions and made Einstein world-famous.
The book has three parts: the special theory, the general theory, and some thoughts on the universe as a whole. It uses almost no mathematics beyond simple algebra, and a great many trains.

full.text: Two principles that seem to clash

items: The principle of relativity: the laws of nature are the same for every observer moving steadily, without turning or speeding up. A passenger in a smooth train cannot tell by any experiment inside it whether it is moving.
The constancy of the speed of light: light in empty space travels at the same speed $c$ (about 300,000 km/s) for every such observer, whatever the motion of its source.

full.html: Ordinary experience says speeds add: a man walking forward in a train moves faster relative to the ground than the train does. Apply that to light and the two principles contradict each other. Einstein’s way out was to look again at what we mean by time.

full.text: What does “at the same time” mean?

full.html: Einstein asks the reader to imagine lightning striking the railway embankment at two distant places, A and B, and to say what it means that the two strokes were simultaneous. His answer is a definition you could test: put an observer at the midpoint M, with mirrors so that he can see A and B at once.

full.text: If the observer perceives the two flashes of lightning at the same time, then they are simultaneous.
full.author: Albert Einstein
full.work: Relativity, Part I, Section VIII, On the Idea of Time in Physics

full.html: Now let a long train run along the track. An observer M′ in the middle of the train is beside M at the moment of the strokes, but she is moving toward B. She meets the light from B before the light from A arrives. Since light moves at the same speed for her too, she must conclude that B struck first.

full.name: gb-light-clock
full.cap: Einstein’s train and embankment. Press Play: M sees both flashes together; M′, riding toward B, sees B’s flash first.

full.text: Events which are simultaneous with reference to the embankment are not simultaneous with respect to the train, and vice versa (relativity of simultaneity). Every reference-body (co-ordinate system) has its own particular time; unless we are told the reference-body to which the statement of time refers, there is no meaning in a statement of the time of an event.
full.author: Albert Einstein
full.work: Relativity, Part I, Section IX, The Relativity of Simultaneity

full.text: Slow clocks, short rods, and E = mc²

full.html: Out of these two principles come the Lorentz transformation and its surprises. A clock moving at speed $v$ runs slow by the factor $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$, and a rod moving lengthwise is shortened by the same factor. No body can be pushed up to the speed of light. And mass and energy turn out to be two forms of one thing, $E = mc^2$.

full.title: Time dilation
full.q: A spaceship passes the Earth at 0.8 c. Its clock records 30 minutes for a trip. How long does the trip take by Earth’s clocks?

full.title: Adding speeds near the speed of light
full.q: On a train moving at 0.6 c, a lamp at the back sends a rocket forward at 0.6 c relative to the train. Galileo’s rule would give 1.2 c. What does Einstein’s rule $w = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c^2)$ give?

full.title: Mass into energy
full.q: How much energy is in 1 gram of mass, by $E = mc^2$?
steps: That is about what a large power station makes in a day.

full.text: The general theory: gravity as geometry

full.html: In Part II Einstein imagines a man inside a closed chest far out in space, pulled steadily upward by a rope. Objects he lets go fall to the floor, exactly as on Earth. No experiment inside can tell whether he is being pulled or resting in a gravitational field. This is the principle of equivalence. It leads to the idea that gravity is not a force in the old sense but the curving of space and time by matter, so that the geometry of space becomes a question for measurement (compare Poincaré, two rungs back).

The theory made three famous predictions: the extra turning of Mercury’s orbit (43 seconds of arc per century, which Newton’s theory could not explain), the bending of starlight passing the Sun (confirmed in the 1919 eclipse), and the reddening of light climbing out of a strong gravitational field (confirmed later). Gravitational waves, another prediction, were first detected directly in 2015.

Relativity does not say “everything is relative.” Its starting point is something absolute: the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same for everyone. What becomes relative is the measure of time and length between events.

Thinking the slow clock is an illusion or a fault in the clock. Every kind of clock, from atoms to heartbeats, is affected the same way. Fast particles called muons, made high in the atmosphere, live long enough to reach the ground only because their time runs slow as seen from Earth.

items: Galileo, earlier on this ladder, first stated that a steady motion can’t be felt from inside a ship’s cabin. Einstein extended Galileo’s principle to light.
Newton assumed an absolute time flowing the same for all. Einstein gave that up, and showed that Newton’s laws are an excellent approximation at low speeds.
Faraday and Maxwell’s electromagnetism, with its fixed speed of light, set the puzzle that relativity solved.
Poincaré had reached parts of the special theory at about the same time.
Eddington, the next rung, tested general relativity in 1919 and wrote about the expanding universe it allowed.
If two observers disagree about which event came first, is there any fact of the matter?
How can a theory overturn our everyday ideas of time and still agree with everyday experience?
Einstein begins with thought experiments, not laboratories. When can thinking alone tell us about the world?

questions: Have you ever sat in a train or car and thought you were moving when it was the one next to you? What does that show?
Why do you think Einstein used trains and lightning to explain his ideas?
If clocks on a fast spaceship run slow, who is “really” older at the end of a trip? Talk it through.
Einstein said the laws of nature are the same for everyone. Why is that a kind of fairness in physics?
Which seems stranger to you: that time can stretch, or that gravity is the shape of space?
